place.excerpt: The Hawaiian story of fire finding is one of the least marvelous of all the legends. Hina, Maui's mother, wanted fish. One morning early Maui saw that the great storm waves of the sea had died down and the fishing grounds could be easily reached. He awakened his brothers and with them hastened to the beach. This was at Kaupo on the island of Maui.
place.note: Verbatim prose from Westervelt's early twentieth-century English compilation. Retain the named island/version; this is not a direct transcription of one oral performance.

fire.work: Legends of Ma-Ui, a Demi God of Polynesia and of his Mother Hina
fire.author: W. D. Westervelt
fire.locator: Chapter V · MAUI FINDING FIRE.; Chapter V · MAUI FINDING FIRE., normalized characters 9620-10676
fire.excerpt: The bird told the demi-god to rub the stalks of water plants together. He guarded the bird and tried the plants. Water instead of fire ran out of the twisted stems. Then she told him to rub reeds together--but they bent and broke and could make no fire. He twisted her neck until she was half dead--then she cried out: "I have hidden the fire in a green stick." Maui worked hard, but not a spark of fire appeared. Again he caught his prisoner by the head and wrung her neck, and she named a kind of dry wood. Maui rubbed the sticks together, but they only became warm. The neck twisting process was resumed--and repeated again and again, until the mud-hen was almost dead--and Maui had tried tree after tree. At last Maui found fire. Then as the flames rose he said: "There is one more thing to rub." He took a fire stick and rubbed the top of the head of his prisoner until the feathers fell off and the raw flesh appeared. Thus the Hawaiian mud-hen and her descendants have ever since had bald heads, and the Hawaiians have had the secret of fire making.

narrativeBlocks.title: Repeated attempts
narrativeBlocks.body: Maui tests different plants and woods after the mud-hen reveals that fire is hidden in a green stick. The account links the legend to rubbing wood to make fire.

narrativeBlocks.title: This is one Hawaiian version
narrativeBlocks.body: Westervelt distinguishes the Hawaiian story from other versions in which Hina may be a grandmother or the fire-giver's role differs. Do not treat the compilation as a uniform Polynesian practice.

narrativeBlocks.title: A practical art in narrative form
narrativeBlocks.body: The episode explains fire-making through Maui's struggle with the mud-hen, in a story Westervelt specifically labels Hawaiian.
